extracted.intended_audience: PR professionals, startup founders, small business owners, and solo communicators doing media outreach
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and sending short, personalized email pitches to journalists to earn media coverage, including finding contacts, timing, follow-ups, and use of PR tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Personalization is non-negotiable. Journalists can spot a copy-paste job from a mile away and it’s one of the fastest ways to get ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention the journalist’s recent work, reference their beat, or acknowledge timing/relevance (examples: “I loved your piece on microplastics...” ; “I saw you often cover sustainable design...” ; “With the holiday season coming up…”). Use tools to personalize at scale but keep a human tone; avoid generic opens like “Dear journalist.” Anti-patterns: mass 'Dear journalist' intros and tokenized personalization that reads copy/pasted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists get a lot of emails. They don’t want to read a manifesto. Keep your pitch under 200 words if possible. Use short paragraphs. Stick to the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a simple framework: Subject line, Opening line (why you’re reaching out), The story (what’s new/relevant), Call to action (interview? coverage? reply?), Link (press release/newsroom/images). No jargon, no filler. Use bullets for key facts. Aim for plain, direct language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject line (clarity, not clickbait)
rubrics_metrics.description: This line determines whether your email gets opened or ignored. Avoid clickbait. Focus on clarity and brevity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good examples: “Study: Gen Z freelancers more likely to use AI than any other group”; “Pitch: Interview with the founder of a zero-waste packaging startup”; “New app helps parents manage screen time, backed by clinical research.” Bad examples: “Press release from our company”; “Exciting opportunity for media coverage”; “Please consider this story.” Rule: be specific about the beat/topic rather than vague.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story angle (reader-first framing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good pitch isn’t about your company. It’s about the story you’re offering and why the journalist’s readers should care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before pitching ask: Who is this for? Why should readers care? How is this different? Tie the angle to trends, news cycles, or common pain points. Example given: a meditation app is only newsworthy if it’s targeted (e.g., for neurodivergent teens) and backed by relevant evidence or unique access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing (when to send)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the best pitch can flop if it lands at the wrong time. Timing affects outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General timing: avoid Mondays; midweek mornings (Tuesday–Thursday, 9–11am) are best; steer clear of Friday afternoons and holidays. Consider time zones and local deadlines. Pitch ahead of relevant events or seasons (e.g., gift guides start months earlier). Offer embargoed stories when appropriate so journalists can prep. Meet deadlines—pitching too late can miss the story window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting vs mass pitching
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass pitching (the same pitch to 100 journalists) is ineffective and damages results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build segmented media lists and tailor messages to the right outlets and reporters. The article calls the scattergun approach never the answer. Use tools to help but prioritize relevance over scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid information overload
rubrics_metrics.description: Dumping everything you know into an email makes you look clueless about what journalists need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stick to essentials, use bullets for key facts, link to a press release or newsroom rather than attaching full documents. Anti-pattern: 1,000-word emails with multiple logos and attachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: One pitch and never following up is a missed opportunity; being overly aggressive can backfire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended cadence: wait 3–5 days after the initial email, send one short, friendly follow-up, and don’t follow up more than twice unless you get a reply. Example follow-up: “Hi [Name], just flagging this in case it got buried. Let me know if you’d like more info or images!”

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect journalist preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists have individual preferences for format, tone, and attachments; failing to respect them harms relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check bios, past stories, or social profiles for stated preferences (e.g., prefers bullet points, no attachments, DMs). If a journalist says “Please don’t send attachments,” don’t send attachments. Avoid invasive personalization (don’t stalk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding and contacting journalists (sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before pitching you need to find the right journalists and contact details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use media databases (note: can be expensive/outdated), LinkedIn, Google News bylines, Substack newsletters, email discovery tools (Hunter.io, RocketReach), and social media where journalists often share contact info. Learn how to verify contacts and pick beat-appropriate targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify email addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirming emails reduces bounces and wasted outreach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use verification tools like Prezly, NeverBounce, Hunter Email Verifier to check validity before sending large outreach campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use PR tools to scale and track outreach
rubrics_metrics.description: Tools can make pitching less chaotic and more measurable without sacrificing personalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capabilities to leverage: build dynamic media lists (tag by beat/location/past coverage), send multimedia pitches (embed images/videos/quotes/links without bulky attachments), track email performance (opens/clicks/replies), collaborate with team members, host a branded newsroom. Benefits: data-driven follow-ups, cleaner sending, centralized assets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear call to action
rubrics_metrics.description: Every pitch should tell the journalist what you want them to do next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state the desired next step (short interview, reply for more info, coverage link) and make it easy to act (provide links to press release, images, background). Keep the ask simple and specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link to press release/online newsroom instead of pasting
rubrics_metrics.description: A pitch is a teaser; press releases contain the details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link to your press release, online newsroom, or asset library rather than copying full press releases into the email or sending heavy attachments. This keeps the pitch concise and gives journalists easy access to background materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer niche outlets when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Niche publications are often more likely to pick up your story than national outlets, especially for early-stage or specialized stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target publications whose audience matches your story; niche relevance often beats broader outreach. Use targeted lists and beats rather than aiming only for big names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Email formatting and asset handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Format influences readability and whether a journalist engages with the pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short paragraphs, bullets for key facts, avoid heavy attachments, embed multimedia when possible via links or platforms that support inline assets. Keep the tone human and avoid robotic-sounding copy (e.g., obvious chatbot output).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inappropriate personalization (don’t stalk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Personalization should be professional and relevant; overly invasive personalization is counterproductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dig into journalists’ private lives or use irrelevant personal details to personalize. Keep personalization focused on their published work, beat, and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch with strategy (media calendar & goals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every pitch should fit into a broader media strategy rather than being a one-off panic email.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define goals (brand narrative, target audience), build a media calendar, and align pitches to longer-term strategy. Ask how each pitch supports brand objectives and audience reach.
